text: Start where Hyde Park starts.
Not with street numbers.
With prairie and marsh, sloping down to the lake.
Sand ridges hold bur oaks.
Swales hold wildflowers.
The grassland runs flat to the horizon.
The water sits close, and the ground stays wet most of the year.
And people already live here.
The Potawatomi hold this land in common with the Ojibwe and the Odawa,
an alliance they call the Council of Three Fires.
One elder, reading the old scrolls, traces that council back to the 790s,
near the straits of Michilimackinac.
The three nations split the work.
The Ojibwe keep the faith.
The Odawa keep the trade.
The Potawatomi keep the fire.
They hunt, trade, and live along these shores for generations,
long before any deed exists to describe them.
The water is what draws outsiders in.
A few miles northwest runs the Chicago Portage,
a low seven-mile stretch of wet ground that floods into a shallow basin the traders call Mud Lake.
In a wet season, a canoe floats almost from the Great Lakes to the Mississippi.
Only a short carry separates the two watersheds.
People work that crossing for centuries.
Then, in the summer of 1673, Kaskaskia guides lead a French fur trader, Louis Jolliet,
and a Jesuit priest, Jacques Marquette,
back up the Illinois and the Des Plaines and over the portage.
They become the first Europeans known to stand on the site of Chicago.
Jolliet sees it at once.
One short canal could join the lake to the river,
and the whole interior of the continent to the sea.
Digging it would take 175 years.
